To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease had more frequently the following mental disorders: Alzheimer's phobias, irritable weakness and mild cognitive impairment.

the first-degree relatives (children and siblings) of patients with AD are more often diagnosed with Alzheimer's phobia (1.5 times more frequent) and mild cognitive impairment (2 times more common), including difficulties in recollection and difficulties in learning new material, reduced sustained attention due fatigue, and the combination of these cognitive deficits (3 times more frequent).
the higher frequency of mental disorders was found among the relatives of patients with AD, including cognitive and non-cogntive disorders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of the genetic and environmental factors in the etiology of AD.
the study of the mental state of the first-degree relatives (FDR) of patients with AD and the analysis of the prevalence of mental disorders in the FDR of patients with AD.
the study of the frequency of mental disorders of cognitive and no-cognitive spectrum in first-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cognitive and non-cogntive spectrum mental disorders are more frequent in the first degree relatives of AD patients.

the cognitive deficit of first-degree relatives of probands with AD is not a specific feature of the disease but is rather a nonspecific manifestation of a number of different mental disorders of the cognitive and noncognitive spectrum.
the relatives of probands with AD have a higher risk of developing mental disorders with cognitive and non-cogntive spectrum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cognitive deficit of the first-degree relatives is a marker of the genetic risk of AD, which is associated with a higher risk of the development of the disease.
the cognitive deficit is the common denominator for all mental disorders of cognitive and/or non-cognitive spectrum, which can be detected in the first-degree relative of AD patients.
the first-degree relatives with AD are more likely to suffer from mental disorders with the spectrum of cognitive and noncognitive disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the relatives of patients with AD have higher risk of developing cognitive and non-cognition mental disorders, which should be considered in the process of clinical and genetic studies of the AD pathogenesis.
the first-degree relatives with cognitive and non-cognition disorders of spectrum can be used in the clinical studies of AD and other dementias.
the relatives of AD patients are at higher risk of developing mental disorders of cognitive and/or non-cognitive spectrum.
